outcome: The general problem is still open and the exact value of N(d,k) is still unknown for most pairs. Since 26 January 2024 the lower bounds for many specific (d,k) pairs have moved, mostly in 2026 and mostly by human-run computer or algebraic constructions, several with AI involvement: Mizuno (June 2026) found N(12,5) >= 34,992 and N(16,5) >= 147,456 with ChatGPT; Cames van Batenburg and Korsky (August 2026) proved that lim n_k(d)/d^k = 1 for each fixed k, resolving a conjecture of Bollobas, with GPT-5.6 Pro credited with one suggestion; de Messieres (October 2026) posted seven improved bounds whose search programs were written by Claude. The degree-57, diameter-2 Moore graph case (N(57,2) = 3250?) is still unresolved; the only nonexistence proof (Makhnev, 2020) is disputed and has no published resolution found.
problem_asks: Read from the statement alone. (1) For every pair of positive integers d and k, the largest possible order N(d,k) of a graph with maximum degree at most d and diameter k: the exact value of this function, for all pairs. (2) For each pair, what a largest graph looks like (the statement asks 'what is the largest graph', so the extremal graph itself is asked for, not only its order). Notes on the wording: the statement says 'diameter k' while the literature standardly uses diameter at most k, and the statement does not say 'undirected' or 'simple'; the directed-graph version is a different question. The statement does not single out the Moore-bound cases, but the case (d,k) = (57,2), where the Moore bound 3250 would be attained, is one of the pairs covered by (1) and is the single pair the Wikipedia article names as open in its lead.

events.what_happened: Ryosuke Mizuno, single author, arXiv:2606.15860, 'New lower bounds for the degree/diameter problem via interaction with a browser-accessible LLM'. Gives explicit graphs with N(12,5) >= 34,992 (12-regular, on 144 * 3^5 vertices) and N(16,5) >= 147,456 (16-regular, on 144 * 4^5 vertices), improving the previously recorded 29,621 and 132,496. The graphs are lifts of a 144-vertex 4-regular controller over the group C4 x C6 with affine maps over F_3 and F_4. Method: a six-day dialogue with ChatGPT in its standard web interface.
events.revisions: v1 14 Jun 2026 only, per the arXiv submission history. Search snippets gave 11 June 2026; the arXiv page gives 14 June and that is used here. Later preprint-level changes are not visible.
events.delivers: Lower bounds only, for two pairs: N(12,5) >= 34,992 and N(16,5) >= 147,456. Both are lower bounds on the named quantity N(d,k) at specific pairs; neither is an exact value. Its own abstract states the bounds with 'greater than or equal to' and its appendix states them strictly; the strict form follows from a diameter argument the paper gives.
events.remains: The exact value of N(12,5) and N(16,5), and N(d,k) for all other pairs, including (57,2). Everything in problem_asks apart from the two stated lower bounds is open.

Appendix A.6 gives the F_3 and F_4 route charts. Degree and diameter can be checked by breadth-first search from every vertex, which the author's repository describes.

events.object: An explicit 12-regular graph on 34,992 vertices with maximum degree 12 and diameter 5, and an explicit 16-regular graph on 147,456 vertices with diameter 5. Both are lifts of a 6-vertex 4-regular base multigraph over the group C4 x C6, with route-chart affine maps over F_3 and F_4 in dimension 5. Explicit, not an existence proof. The paper's own comparison gives the Moore bound for (12,5) as 193,261, so 34,992 is about 18 percent of it.

systems.name: gpt-5-5-pro
systems.what_it_did: Generated the candidate construction in a long web-interface dialogue. The paper states: 'Candidate generation itself was left mainly to the LLM' (section 4.1); 'Rather than directly guessing the whole final graph, the LLM reformulated the task' (section 4.6); the route-chart lift principle 'first appeared' in Round 023, after the user requested 'an a priori mathematical reason to expect success' and asked the LLM 'to devise a new principle' (sections 4.3 and 5.3). The author's own framing: 'This paper does not treat ChatGPT as an author or as an autonomous prover' and 'ChatGPT was used as an interactive discovery engine' (section 1). This is the load-bearing AI involvement: the construction was produced in the dialogue.

events.what_happened: Wouter Cames van Batenburg and Samuel Korsky, arXiv:2608.03965, 'Asymptotically attaining the Moore bound'. For each fixed positive integer k, the maximum order n_k(d) of a graph with maximum degree at most d and diameter at most k satisfies n_k(d)/d^k -> 1 as d -> infinity. The paper says this 'resolv[es] the asymptotic degree-diameter problem for fixed diameter and prov[es] a conjecture of Bollobas', and treats the edge-count analogue (Corollary 1.2), which resolves a conjecture of Cambie, Cames van Batenburg, de Joannis de Verclos and Kang. Lower bound from regular graphs H_{k,q} (halved-flag graphs) on partial flags of F_q^(2k+1).
events.revisions: Single version v1, submitted 4 Aug 2026, per the arXiv submission history. The Lean formalization README says it was formalized from the 3 August 2026 draft and that no mathematically relevant changes were made before submission.
events.delivers: For every fixed k: lim_{d->infinity} n_k(d)/d^k = 1, i.e. n_k(d) ~ d^k as the degree grows. This covers the asymptotic behaviour of N(d,k) in d, with k fixed, for all fixed k. It does not give exact values, and it says nothing about any fixed pair (d,k). The Lean formalization covers Lemma 2.1, Proposition 3.1, Theorem 1.1, Lemma 4.1 and Corollary 1.2, and the README lists as outside its kernel-checked scope the explicit O_k(q^-1) and O_k(q^-2) error rates and a bipartite-restricted exact limit that depends on a cited external bound.
events.remains: Exact values of N(d,k) for every pair, including (57,2). The rate at which n_k(d)/d^k approaches 1 and the explicit error terms as stated in the README's exclusions. The degree-57 Moore graph case is untouched.

events.directly_checkable: The lower-bound graphs H_{k,q} are explicit: vertices are even-rank partial flags of F_q^(2k+1), and two vertices are adjacent when they share a compatible odd-rank partial flag. The paper states they are regular of diameter k and have order (1+o(1)) Delta^k.
events.direction: Proves the asymptotic statement conjectured by Bollobas (the limsup form, and the stronger full limit). Cuts in favour of the Moore bound being asymptotically sharp for fixed k as d grows. No exact value and no contradiction with any conjectured value.
events.object: The regular graphs H_{k,q}, indexed by prime powers q, built from partial flags in F_q^(2k+1), with diameter k and order (1+o(1)) Delta(H_{k,q})^k. Explicit (no existence argument). Attached to the proof of the main theorem as its lower-bound family.

systems.name: GPT-5.6 Pro
systems.what_it_did: Suggested the idea of splitting complete flags into their odd- and even-rank subflags, which the authors say was initially discussed for the edge problem; the authors developed that suggestion into the halved-flag construction H_{k,q}, which supplies the lower bound in Theorem 1.1. The paper says the model was used 'during exploratory brainstorming about possible constructions' and that the discussion was directed by the authors. The authors state they 'formulated and verified all mathematical arguments, and take full responsibility for the content'. The load-bearing question for the later pass: the model supplied a construction principle, and the authors built the proof on it; the authors call it a suggestion, not a proof.

The record does not say that the AI devised the voltage-lift or generalized-quadrangle constructions. Whether writing search code counts as load-bearing is for the later pass: the graphs were found by the programs, but the mathematical families are not attributed to the AI.

events.what_happened: Kelly Isham (Colgate), Kartik Lakhotia (Intel), Laura Monroe (Los Alamos), Fabrizio Petrini (Intel), arXiv:2608.27253, 'Kronecker Products, Polarity Quotients and Large Graph Constructions'. Builds three families of large graphs of diameter 2, 3 and 5 from a structural compatibility between Kronecker products of bipartite polarity graphs, using generalized polygons G_n(q,q) as factors. Table 1 gives new diameter-3 graphs at degrees 18, 19, 20 of orders 2340, 2470, 2600, against 1620, 1638, 1958 in the Degree-Diameter Table and 1830, 2128, 2394 for PolarStar. The abstract says the diameter-3 family from generalized quadrangles gives graphs 'larger than any previously known at their degrees'.
events.revisions: Single version v1, 27 Aug 2026.
events.delivers: New lower bounds for N(d,3) at degrees 18, 19 and 20 (2340, 2470, 2600), and families of graphs for an infinite but sparse set of degrees with diameters 2, 3 and 5. The families approach a theoretical upper bound as the polygon parameters grow. Each is a bound at specific degrees or a sparse family of degrees, and no exact value is established.
events.remains: Exact values for all pairs; the diameter-2 and diameter-5 families are asymptotic on a sparse set of degrees only.
events.directly_checkable: The constructions are described explicitly (Kronecker products of polarity quotients of generalized polygon incidence graphs); degree and diameter are checkable by breadth-first search.
events.direction: Raises lower bounds for N(d,3) at degrees 18, 19 and 20, and gives sparse-degree families for diameters 2, 3 and 5. Cuts in the same direction as other lower-bound events.
events.object: Explicit graphs from Kronecker products of bipartite polarity graphs with generalized quadrangle factors G_n(q,q); the diameter-3 graphs at degrees 18, 19, 20 with orders 2340, 2470, 2600. Explicit.

events.what_happened: Paul Stankovski Wagner, arXiv:2610.04815, 'Less is Moore' (cs.DM and math.CO). Exact search for radius-two Moore trees, the structure whose completion gives a diameter-2 Moore graph. The paper says it is 'not an attempt to settle that open problem'. It gives algorithm-engineering improvements (short-cycle pruning, bit-parallel domains, symmetry-based pruning): on a k = 9 benchmark the wall time drops from 47.6 s to 17.9 s; a five-minute degree-57 stress run peaks at 161 MiB.
events.revisions: Single version v1, 3 Oct 2026, per the abstract page.
events.delivers: Speed-ups for an exact search for diameter-2 Moore graphs. No new bound on N(d,k) and no result on whether any Moore graph of degree 57 exists. The k = 9 and degree-57 runs are benchmarks, not results.
events.remains: The whole problem, including the degree-57 existence question.

machine_checked.system: Exact exhaustive computer search; described as tested by controlled regression tests

events.direction: Does not bear on the answer to the statement; it concerns the efficiency of a search for the degree-57 Moore graph.

events.what_happened: Yawara Ishida, arXiv:2606.29183, 'No involutions in the missing Moore graph' (math.CO). Claims that a Moore graph of degree 57 (on 3250 vertices, strongly regular with parameters (3250,57,0,1)), if it exists, has no involutory automorphisms, so its automorphism group has odd order. The argument uses a trace-rank identity from the Brauer quotient of p-permutation lattices, applied to strongly regular graphs.
events.revisions: v1 28 Jun 2026; v2 8 Jul 2026 (current, 22 KB).
events.delivers: A restriction on the automorphism group of a hypothetical degree-57 Moore graph: no involutions. It is conditional on existence and establishes neither existence nor nonexistence, and it does not change any bound on N(d,k).
events.remains: Whether a Moore graph of degree 57 exists, i.e. whether N(57,2) = 3250; and all other pairs.
events.direction: Restricts a hypothetical object to odd-order automorphism groups; cuts neither for nor against existence.

events.what_happened: Derek H. Smith and Roberto Montemanni, 'The Moore Graph of Diameter 2 and Degree 57 via Cyclic Derangements', Axioms, published 1 May 2026 (DOI 10.3390/axioms15050332). Per search snippets, the paper shows that a construction using only a cyclic group of permutations (a cyclic group of derangements) cannot produce the degree-57 Moore graph; other groups of derangements, and non-group sets, remain open. NOT OPENED: the MDPI page returned HTTP 403 on both the DOI and the redirect target.
events.revisions: Not known beyond the publication date in the search snippet (received February 2026, accepted late April 2026).
events.delivers: Per the abstract snippet only: rules out the cyclic-group route for the degree-57 Moore graph. Does not establish existence or nonexistence; the authors discuss other groups as open.
events.remains: Existence of the degree-57 Moore graph; all other pairs.
events.direction: Rules out one construction route; the question remains open.

events.what_happened: Smith and Montemanni, 'Potential Subgraphs of the Missing Moore Graph', Symmetry 16(12), article 1563, a computational study of partial structures of a degree-57 Moore graph under a cyclic-group ansatz, reported via search snippet as extending a previously known sequence of 15 such subgraphs to 20 using the Google OR-Tools CP-SAT solver. NOT OPENED: the MDPI and University of Modena PDF pages returned HTTP 403. Date taken from the volume and issue in the URL.
events.delivers: Per the snippet only: extends a partial-structure census for the degree-57 case. No bound on N(57,2) and no existence or nonexistence result.
events.remains: Existence of the degree-57 Moore graph; all other pairs.
events.direction: Partial structures only; neither cuts for nor against existence.

events.what_happened: Smith and Montemanni, 'EURO Journal on Computational Optimization' (January 2023 issue, per DOAJ listing; article title not opened), an optimization study of the degree-57 Moore graph. Per search snippets, the algorithm converges to solutions 'massively short' of the required number of edges, and the authors suggest the graph may not exist. NOT OPENED (DOAJ listing only).
events.delivers: Heuristic evidence against existence, per the snippet; not a proof, and does not settle N(57,2).
events.remains: Existence or nonexistence of the degree-57 Moore graph; all other pairs.
events.doubts: Heuristic only; the snippet says the authors suggest but do not prove nonexistence.
events.direction: Heuristic evidence against existence of a degree-57 Moore graph, not a result.

events.what_happened: A. A. Makhnev, arXiv:2010.13443, 'Moore graph with parameters (3250,57,0,1) does not exist' (Russian text, English abstract). Claims that a distance-regular graph with intersection array {55,54,2;1,1,54} does not exist, and concludes that no Moore graph of degree 57 exists, via the Jurisic-Vidali reduction. Related journal paper: A. A. Makhnev and D. V. Paduchikh, 'The largest Moore graph and a distance-regular graph with intersection array {55,54,2;1,1,54}', Algebra i Logika 59(4), 2020 (not opened).
events.revisions: v1 26 Oct 2020; v2 9 Nov 2020 (current).
events.delivers: Claims to settle the (57,2) pair: no Moore graph of degree 57, i.e. N(57,2) < 3250. Only the (57,2) pair is affected; the rest of problem_asks is untouched.
events.remains: All pairs other than (57,2) (the claim is about the one pair). Within (57,2), the claim is contested (see doubts).
events.doubts: Vance Faber and Jonathan Keegan (arXiv:2210.09577, 2022-2023) argue that the case analysis appears to be flawed and that 'this seems not to be correct'; they reduce the question to an equivalent family of permutation systems and find the system of equations factors into blocks that each have solutions. No published resolution of this dispute was found. The Renteln erratum (see renteln-2015-erratum-2021) concerns a different paper's Theorem 3.1 and does not address Makhnev's argument.
events.direction: Claims nonexistence of a degree-57 Moore graph, which would settle the (57,2) pair in the direction that no Moore graph exists.

events.what_happened: Vance Faber and Jonathan Keegan, arXiv:2210.09577, 'Existence of a Moore graph of degree 57 is still open'. Argues that the 2020 Makhnev nonexistence argument 'seems not to be correct' because the system of equations factors into small diagonal blocks, each with solutions, and gives an alternative formulation: the Moore graph exists if and only if some member of a family of permutation systems has no solutions.
events.delivers: Establishes no new bound and no existence or nonexistence result. It is a critique of the (57,2) nonexistence argument and a reformulation of the existence question.
events.remains: Existence of the degree-57 Moore graph; all other pairs.
events.direction: Cuts against the Makhnev nonexistence claim; no direction on existence.

events.what_happened: Paul Renteln, 'Some constraints on the missing Moore graph' (arXiv:1509.00327, 2015; published Australasian Journal of Combinatorics 77(3), pp. 373-382). Derives constraints that a hypothetical degree-57 Moore graph would have to satisfy (biregular bipartitions, automorphisms). An erratum in Australasian Journal of Combinatorics 79(1) (2021), pp. 193-194, says the proof of Theorem 3.1 contained a computational error that rendered it invalid; the main Corollary 3.1 stands, and later results need equal-part bipartitions. Not opened: search snippets only.
events.revisions: Erratum 2021 (Australasian Journal of Combinatorics 79(1), 193-194).
events.delivers: Constraints on a hypothetical degree-57 Moore graph; no existence or nonexistence result.
events.remains: Existence of the degree-57 Moore graph; all other pairs.
events.doubts: Theorem 3.1 contained a computational error per the 2021 erratum; the erratum credits Megan Boes with flagging it. The corrected statement is narrower.
events.direction: Constraints on a hypothetical object; no direction on existence.

events.what_happened: Antoine Dailly, Sasha Darmon, Ugo Giocanti, Claire Hilaire and Petru Valicov, arXiv:2507.18797, 'Largest planar graphs of diameter 3 and fixed maximum degree -- connection with fractional matchings'. For planar graphs of maximum degree at most Delta and diameter at most 3, the maximum order is (9/2)Delta up to an additive constant; this matches the Fellows, Hell and Seyffarth lower bound.
events.revisions: v1 24 Jul 2025 per the abstract page.
events.delivers: Settles the diameter-3 planar restriction: max order (9/2)Delta + O(1) for planar graphs. This is a restricted class (planar graphs), not the general problem; the general N(Delta,3) is not moved.
events.remains: The general problem for all graphs, including the general diameter-3 values.
events.direction: Discarded for scope. A planar-restriction result on a neighbouring question; it does not change what the entry for the general problem should say.

events.what_happened: Lakhotia, Monroe, Isham, Besta, Blach, Hoefler and Petrini, 'PolarStar: Expanding the Scalability Horizon of Diameter-3 Networks', arXiv:2302.07217 (Feb 2023), SPAA 2024. Diameter-3 networks from a star product of an Erdos-Renyi polarity graph ER_q with an Inductive-Quad or Paley supernode; asymptotically reaches an 8/27 fraction of the diameter-3 Moore bound for the degrees it covers. Not opened: search snippet only.
events.revisions: arXiv v2 and the SPAA 2024 version differ in comparison figures (per snippet).
events.delivers: Lower bounds on N(d,3) for infinitely many d (degrees of the form q+1 and their star-product splits). Pre-window background against which the 2026 diameter-3 entries are compared.
events.remains: Exact values; all other degrees.
events.direction: Lower bounds at infinitely many diameter-3 degrees; no conflict with any conjectured value.

events.what_happened: Chishwashwa, Faber and Streib, arXiv:2405.12374, 'Algebraic Constructions for the Digraph Degree-Diameter Problem' (first submitted May 2024; v3 1 Oct 2025). Constructs digraphs via quasigroups, 1-factors and permutation groups. Not opened: search snippet only.
events.revisions: v3 1 Oct 2025 (per snippet).
events.delivers: Constructions for the directed version of the problem. This is a different question (digraphs, not graphs), so it moves no bound on the statement's quantity.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks.
events.direction: Discarded for scope: directed graphs.

events.what_happened: Araujo-Pardo, Conder, Garcia-Colin, Kiss and Leemans, arXiv:2401.15539, 'A note on girth-diameter cages', submitted 28 January 2024 (v1). Studies (k; g, d)-graphs, k-regular with girth g and diameter d, and shows n0(k;5,4) >= k^2+k+2 with cages determined for k = 3, 4, 5. Not opened: search listing only.
events.revisions: v1 28 Jan 2024; journal version in The Art of Discrete and Applied Mathematics 8(3), 2025 (per search).
events.delivers: Results on a different problem (cages with a diameter condition, girth 5, diameter 4). Not the degree-diameter problem for graphs of max degree at most d and diameter k. Discarded for scope.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks.
events.direction: Discarded for scope: a regular-graph girth-diameter problem.

disputes.summary: Same values, two credits. The orders 88,452 for (14,5) and 100,000 for (15,5) are in Mizuno's repository (no visible date) and are credited in the Comellas table to Sami Badaoui on 16 and 19 August 2026. Neither the repository date nor the Badaoui source was established, so priority is not settled.

Chain of (12,5) records in 2026: Comellas 2024 29,621 (leapsinbounds, Jun 2024); Mizuno 34,992 (arXiv 14 Jun 2026; table credit 25 Jul 2026); Rajiv 38,167 (Zenodo 23 Sep 2026); Rajiv 41,699 (Zenodo 30 Sep 2026); the table currently shows 42,342 credited to Rajiv in September 2026. A search snippet earlier reported 38,167 as the table value; the table page read on 11 Oct 2026 shows 42,342. The current table value is taken from the page; the snippet is not relied on.
Mizuno's arXiv v1 is dated 14 June 2026 on the arXiv abstract page. Search snippets gave 11 June 2026; the arXiv page is taken as correct.
Rajiv's Zenodo 'Cayley graphs, orbit graphs and lifts' record shows 24 Sep 2026; the Comellas table bibliography dates it 30 Sep 2026. The Zenodo date is used.

The Comellas table dates the (10,5) entry to Rajiv on 24 Aug 2026, but the 33,397-vertex graph for (10,5) is in Rajiv's 23 Sep 2026 record. The table credit date and the Zenodo date do not match; the Zenodo date is used.
The EJGTA 2025 abstract says fourteen new graphs; the Mendeley dataset notes list thirteen pairs found in 2024. Not resolved here; the paper's pair list was not opened.

Yang and Zhu (2019), 'fractal block design' nonexistence claim for the degree-57 Moore graph, was mentioned in one search snippet. The arXiv id given for it (1910.05989) is a different paper, 'The classification of local m-GCI-group on finite nonabelian simple groups' (Zhu and Yang), and the claim could not be located. Recorded here as unresolved, not as an event.

Makhnev's 2020 paper is credited in one search snippet to Makhnev and Paduchikh's 2020 Algebra i Logika paper, which treats the same intersection array {55,54,2;1,1,54}. The arXiv paper (2010.13443) is by A. A. Makhnev alone.

summary: The problem asks for the exact value of the largest order N(d,k) for every pair of positive integers, and for the extremal graphs. Nothing has settled it since 26 January 2024: no exact value of N(d,k) has been established for any pair not already known, and the degree-57, diameter-2 Moore graph case is still open. What has happened is a large number of lower-bound improvements at specific pairs, most of them in 2026. The earliest in-window event is the 2024 update to the Comellas table (arXiv:2406.18994, 27 June 2024), which raised N(12,5) from 29,470 to 29,621 and thirteen other pairs; its 2025 journal version (EJGTA, accepted 2 April 2025) reports fourteen graphs. In 2026 the bounds move steadily. Mizuno (arXiv:2606.15860, 14 June 2026) gives N(12,5) >= 34,992 and N(16,5) >= 147,456 from a six-day ChatGPT dialogue (gpt-5-5-pro in the transcript metadata); the construction is load-bearing per the author's own account ('Candidate generation itself was left mainly to the LLM'). Rajiv posted a run of Zenodo preprints from July to September 2026 with lower bounds at many pairs, found by computer searches over Cayley and lift constructions, none of them attributing the work to an AI system; the September papers push N(12,5) to 38,167 and then 41,699, and the Comellas table shows 42,342 for (12,5) at the time of reading. Cames van Batenburg and Korsky (arXiv:2608.03965, 4 August 2026) prove lim n_k(d)/d^k = 1 for each fixed k, which resolves a conjecture of Bollobas; the paper credits GPT-5.6 Pro with suggesting the odd/even subflag splitting that the authors developed into the halved-flag construction (H_{k,q}), which supplies the lower bound in the main theorem. They say they 'formulated and verified all mathematical arguments'. Their Lean 4 formalization is described as AI-assisted without naming the tool. de Messieres (Zenodo, October 2026) gives seven bounds, the search programs for which the record says were 'produced with the help of an AI assistant (Claude, Anthropic)'; the record does not say the AI devised the constructions. Kronecker-product constructions by Isham, Lakhotia, Monroe and Petrini (arXiv:2608.27253, 27 August 2026) give diameter-3 bounds at degrees 18 to 20 with no AI mention. Two degree-57 Moore graph items are recent: Ishida (June 2026) shows no involutory automorphisms if the graph exists, and Wagner (October 2026) improves exact search for diameter-2 Moore trees and says it does not attempt the open problem. Smith and Montemanni (Axioms, 1 May 2026) rule out a cyclic-group route, but I could not open that article (HTTP 403). The only nonexistence claim, Makhnev (arXiv:2010.13443, October 2020), is contested by Faber and Keegan (arXiv:2210.09577, 2022) who argue 'this seems not to be correct'; no published resolution was found. The close calls: (a) whether the Cames suggestion is load-bearing, since the authors call it a suggestion they developed; (b) whether writing the search code for de Messieres's graphs counts, since the mathematical families are not attributed to the AI; (c) the Comellas table's header says 'except for some SageMath scripts that were created with the help of ChatGPT', which I did not treat as a system in the result because it concerns scripts, but it is a disclosure on the table that the judging pass should see. Lower-bound events are reported in the direction of the problem's question; none claims or contradicts an exact value.
competing_reading: The lower-bound events could be read as 'nothing has happened': no pair's exact value has moved, N(d,k) is still unknown for every pair that matters, and the asymptotic result from Cames van Batenburg and Korsky is the only resolution of anything the statement asks, and it is about a limit rather than the largest graph. Read that way, the AI-linked lower bounds at (12,5) and (16,5) are ordinary improvements that were later superseded by human-run constructions in September 2026. In the other direction, the Cames paper could be read as an AI-generated idea at the centre of a resolved conjecture, because the authors credit GPT-5.6 Pro with the suggestion that led to the construction used for the lower bound. Under the second reading the AI is load-bearing; under the first it is a brainstorming aid.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The arXiv PDF and any acknowledgements of 2608.03965 read in full, to see whether the GPT-5.6 Pro suggestion is the idea the proof turns on, or whether H_{k,q} was developed independently. (2) The first-version dates and version histories of the de Messieres Zenodo record and the Rajiv records, and the data-and-verification.zip contents, to see whether any AI credit appears inside the Rajiv data. (3) The Mizuno repository's commit history, to date the 2026 table-linked graphs for (14,5) and (15,5) and settle the Badaoui priority question. (4) The MDPI article (Axioms, 1 May 2026) and the Symmetry 2024 article, both blocked here. (5) The 2024 Comellas EJGTA paper's pair list and whether the 14 graphs were first public in arXiv:2406.18994. (6) Any refereed resolution or replacement of the Faber and Keegan critique of Makhnev's 2020 argument, which would settle the (57,2) case. (7) The Comellas table's history of entries and credits, to date the untagged credits (Yugeswardeenoo, Marosi, Wupperfeld, Badaoui, Isufi, Prajapati, Conder) to specific sources.
